_comment: Every backend declares the platform it runs on, and the launcher only offers the ones that match. Windows archives are zips that extract flat; the macOS and Linux archives are tar.gz files whose contents sit under a llama-b<build> directory, so they declare stripComponents to land flat like the others. A backend may also declare the architecture it was built for, and the launcher then hides it on a machine of the other one: an x64 build is not something an aarch64 board should be offered and then fail to execute. The tree counts are what PowerShell's Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File reports, which on macOS includes the .dylib symlinks: counting them with find(1) instead gives 43 rather than 61 and would fail verification.

cuda13.name: NVIDIA CUDA 13.3 (GeForce RTX 20/30/40/50, Quadro, Tesla)
cuda13._pinDeviceComment: llama.cpp's default split mode is 'layer' over EVERY device the backend enumerates, so a machine with more than one card runs part of the model on a card nobody chose. It sizes that split with the 'free' figure from --list-devices, which is static: measured here, a Vulkan build reported 15227 MiB free on an RTX 5070 Ti while nvidia-smi reported 798, because a training job held the rest. Backends that enumerate hardware they do not own set this, and the launcher then pins one device and sends --split-mode none.

vulkan.name: Vulkan (AMD, Intel and NVIDIA; recommended for APUs and integrated GPUs)
vulkan._pinDeviceComment: llama.cpp's default split mode is 'layer' over EVERY device the backend enumerates, so a machine with more than one card runs part of the model on a card nobody chose. It sizes that split with the 'free' figure from --list-devices, which is static: measured here, a Vulkan build reported 15227 MiB free on an RTX 5070 Ti while nvidia-smi reported 798, because a training job held the rest. Backends that enumerate hardware they do not own set this, and the launcher then pins one device and sends --split-mode none.
vulkan._speculativeComment: Measured twice, and the second measurement is the stronger reason. Originally: the cost of maintaining the draft context cancels the gain. On b10566 it is worse than pointless - Gemma 4 E4B with its companion draft model aborts the process during KV allocation, 'pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l22) in a buffer (Vulkan0) that cannot run the operation (NONE)', which is Gemma 4's shared-KV layers meeting a Vulkan buffer that has no kernel for them. Not measured on Qwen, whose MTP is embedded rather than a separate file and may well be a different story.

vulkan-linux._comment: The Linux counterpart of the Windows Vulkan backend, and the one to pick on any AMD or Intel GPU, an APU, or an NVIDIA card without CUDA installed. The ubuntu archives are tar.gz with the build under a llama-b<build> directory, so they strip one component to land flat, exactly like the macOS one. This backend sits on b10976, the same build as cuda-linux, on purpose: on a machine that carries both an NVIDIA card and an AMD iGPU the two backends get compared against each other, and comparing an older Vulkan against a newer CUDA measures the release as much as it measures the driver. The local archive name carries the build for the same reason - an artifact called llama-vulkan-linux-x64.tar.gz that holds a different build than the config points at is indistinguishable from a truncated download, and Ensure-Artifact would try to resume across two different files.
vulkan-linux.name: Vulkan (AMD, Intel and NVIDIA; recommended for APUs and integrated GPUs)
vulkan-linux._integrityManifestComment: Declared alongside tree, which stays what verification reads, because the two fields do different jobs. The tree count is the contract the committed verifier enforces; the manifest is what makes a version bump self-healing, since Ensure-Backend rebuilds an extracted folder that has no manifest instead of returning early on a folder that merely already has a binary in it. Without that second field a machine that installed the previous build keeps it, and VERIFY.sh reports the new tree as incomplete with no command in this project that fixes it.
vulkan-linux._pinDeviceComment: Same reason as on Windows: llama.cpp splits over every device the backend enumerates, sized with the static 'free' from --list-devices, so a machine with an APU and a discrete card runs part of the model somewhere nobody chose. The launcher pins one device and sends --split-mode none.
vulkan-linux._speculativeComment: Every Linux figure quoted below was taken on the b10566 build this entry carried before the bump to b10976, so read them as the same hardware on an older llama.cpp, not as numbers this binary reproduces. On, and measured here rather than assumed. Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B from its MTP build, 32K with vision and q8_0 KV on a gfx1103 iGPU: 28.2-28.6 tok/s without, 37.5-38.3 with, at draft acceptance 0.71-0.73 - the embedded nextn path works on this backend. That is NOT a clearance for every method: the Windows measurement on this same backend stands, where on b10566 Gemma 4 E4B with its COMPANION DRAFT FILE aborts during KV allocation with 'pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l22) in a buffer (Vulkan0) that cannot run the operation (NONE)', which is Gemma 4's shared-KV layers meeting a Vulkan buffer that has no kernel for them. That path HAS now been run on Linux, with the same b10566 build, and it does not abort: Gemma 4 E4B loads its companion draft, generates and stops cleanly. What it does not do is pay - acceptance 0.34, and generation within noise of no speculation - so the three Gemma entries turn it off for Linux in their own blocks rather than the backend refusing it for everyone.

vulkan-linux-arm64.name: Vulkan (ARM64: Ampere, Grace, Raspberry Pi and other aarch64 boards)

cuda-linux._comment: Shown only when nvidia-smi confirms that the Linux host has a working NVIDIA device. The archive includes llama.cpp; its matching cudart archive supplies the CUDA 13.3 user-space libraries, so users need an NVIDIA driver but do not need a CUDA toolkit. Vulkan and CPU remain available when this check fails.
cuda-linux.name: NVIDIA CUDA 13.3 (GeForce RTX 20/30/40/50, Quadro, Tesla)

metal._comment: Apple Silicon only. There is no CPU-only sibling because there is nothing to gain from one: unified memory means the weights are already where the CPU can read them, so Metal is never the slower choice. Intel Macs would need the macos-x64 archive and are not supported.
metal.name: Apple Metal (M1-M4, unified memory)
metal._speculativeComment: On, so the option exists, with the per-model blocks deciding who actually gets it. One measurement so far: Qwen 3.8 27B with vision on a 24 GiB M4 Pro at 32K gives draft acceptance 0.93, mean draft length 3.79, and generation unchanged at 10.6 tok/s against 10.7 without. The same configuration at 48K ran out of Metal memory during the first decode, after loading cleanly and reporting healthy - which is why that model's macos block carries a measured maxContext. See its mtp block in models.json for why a hybrid attention/SSM architecture cannot profit. The Gemma 4 family is pure sliding-window attention with a small companion draft file, an entirely different shape of bet, and is still untested here: it inherits its CUDA costMiB and has no verified ceiling, so treat the first run of one as an experiment.
